stories.brief: A Jewish literary account of shtetl life describes weekday market trading: shoppers bargain with sellers, while women shopkeepers weigh and wrap goods and use conversation to attract customers.
storyBeats: In his 1919 account, Hillel Zeitlin recalls a weekday market among low wooden houses, narrow streets and wooden shops.
Peasants bring wagons of goods to the market, and horses eat straw from the wagons while Jewish buyers approach to inspect the merchandise.
Buyers ask the prices, bargain, make objections and then buy or sell goods.
Women shopkeepers weigh goods, wrap them and tie the bundles for customers.
To attract buyers, women shopkeepers use requests, gentle words, stories and jokes; the account also describes sharper exchanges with difficult customers or competing shopkeepers.
The shopkeepers’ conversation can include questions about a customer’s health, family, fruit and horses.
Zeitlin portrays some husbands helping in their wives’ shops, while suggesting that shop work does not seem natural to them; they earn a living there nonetheless.
In one busy shop, a husband stands aside reciting prayers he did not finish while his wife moves among customers and goods.
Another shopkeeper is portrayed as discussing a passage of religious study before a purchase and returning to study soon after completing the market deal.
The account describes two large rival shops selling wool, linen, silk, embroidery, clothing, lamps and ornaments for brides and grooms.
